title: AD Contract Breakdown: Ryan Colton, New Hampshire - HERO Sports
content:
Can an athletic director’s contract offer hints about where a university’s priorities lie? It has been a few weeks since New Hampshire announced Ryan Colton as its next athletic director. Colton replaces Allison Rich, who stepped down in July after announcing her departure in April. A closer look at Colton’s contract offers some clues about what UNH values most in its next era of athletics leadership, and where Colton’s own priorities may align. Colton’s five-year agreement is longer and more lucrative than the four-year deal Rich signed in 2022. More interestingly, however, UNH rewrote how its athletic director is rewarded for financial performance, placed significantly greater contractual emphasis on fundraising, strengthened the buyout language should he leave Durham, and inserted protections that appear designed to prevent Colton from being held responsible for certain problems he inherits. None of those provisions independently proves a major strategic shift. Contracts are negotiated documents, and some changes may reflect four years of legal housekeeping. Collectively, though, they provide some clues about what UNH expects from its new athletics administration. Rich received a four-year contract running from July 2022 through June 2026 with an annual base salary of $255,000. Her agreement also included a $20,000 annual supplemental stipend. Colton received a five-year term, running through June 30, 2031, with a base salary of $275,000 and a $25,000 stipend. That puts his stated annual compensation before bonuses at $300,000, compared to $275,000 under Rich’s original agreement. The base salary increase is roughly 8 percent. The additional year may be more meaningful. At a time when UNH President Elizabeth Chilton described college athletics as being at a “pivotal moment,” the university gave its new AD a longer runway to manage it. And UNH made that runway slightly more expensive for both parties to abandon. Rich could receive a financial performance bonus based on “Positive Net Revenue” from the athletics operating fund. The formula paid 3 percent of positive net revenue up to $250,000 and 5 percent above that level, with a maximum financial bonus of $25,000. Colton’s agreement eliminates that formula and essentially creates two separate business-development incentives. Beginning in FY2028, he can earn up to $25,000 for year-over-year growth in controllable revenue, excluding philanthropy, provided he stays within the approved expenditure budget. He can earn an additional $20,000 based on fundraising performance. There is another subtle change … the targets aren’t locked into the contract. Financial metrics will be established annually with UNH’s executive vice president for finance and administration, while philanthropy goals will be established with the vice president for advancement. The president has final approval of both. Instead of simply rewarding an athletics operating surplus, UNH can annually tell its AD: That fits Colton’s background. UNH specifically highlighted his previous work in his introductory press conference when it came to revenue generation. The allocation of bonus dollars changed dramatically. Rich’s academic incentive paid $8,000 for a Graduation Success Rate of at least 85, $10,000 for 90-94, and $12,000 for 95 or higher. Her competitive incentive generally paid $3,000 for a conference championship or NCAA tournament/playoff qualification and $7,500 for a national championship. Colton receives just $3,000 for a GSR of 85, $4,000 for 90-94 and $10,000 for 95-plus. His entire competitive-success category is capped at $10,000 annually. A team conference championship or NCAA berth is worth $2,000, and a team national championship is worth $4,000. UNH didn’t stop rewarding academics or championships. It just simply shifted considerably more upside toward enterprise growth. Colton can earn up to $45,000 annually from the new financial success and philanthropy categories alone. That makes the contract read less like a traditional AD incentive package centered primarily on winning and graduating athletes, and more like one written for the person responsible for running an increasingly complex Division I business … centered on the bottom line. This is the most legally interesting addition, where I also believe Colton, who earned a Juris Doctor degree from New England Law Boston, shows his savviness. Under Rich’s agreement, a major NCAA violation within the UNH athletics program could give the university grounds to terminate the contract, even apart from a finding that Rich personally committed the violation. Colton’s language is more carefully limited, or strategically worded. UNH can terminate him if he is personally involved in a major NCAA violation. But for a broader violation within the athletics program, the contract specifically references a major violation occurring after the beginning of Fiscal Year 2028 that Colton “knew or reasonably should have known” about. The bonus language contains a similar firewall. Certain Level I and Level II violations only affect Colton’s bonus eligibility if they occurred after the beginning of FY2028, unless Colton himself was involved. Colton begins work Aug. 17, 2026. The contract effectively gives the incoming AD substantial protection against being contractually punished for institutional conduct that predates his administration. That is not me suggesting UNH is expecting an NCAA visit or two. What it does suggest is sophisticated risk allocation: Colton is responsible for the department he takes over, but his contract distinguishes between what he inherits and what happens on his watch. For an attorney turned athletic administrator, that’s an interesting negotiated protection. Rich had a declining liquidated damages schedule if she left for another Division I athletics job: 100 percent of base salary in Year 1, 75 percent in Year 2, 50 percent in Year 3, and 25 percent in Year 4. Her agreement also included a detailed process that required presidential permission to explore certain opportunities outside UNH’s conference. Colton’s structure is different and much more financially challenging. He must notify the president in writing (generally as a courtesy) before engaging in discussions or negotiations with another prospective employer. If he leaves for athletics-related employment, he owes 100 percent of his base salary during any of the first three contract years, 90 percent in Year 4 and 80 percent in Year 5. At his initial $275,000 salary, that means the Year 5 exit price would still be $220,000. UNH also added explicit anti-poaching language prohibiting Colton from assisting in recruiting current or prospective student-athletes or staff members to his new employer, with potential damages separate from his contractual buyout. For what it’s worth, that clause is found in many coaches’ contracts but is rarely, if ever, enforceable. Bonus Insight:Despite Colton receiving a five-year deal compared to Rich’s four-year agreement, UNH did not meaningfully increase its guaranteed exposure. Rich’s contract guaranteed one year of her then-current base salary if terminated without cause, which was $255,000 at signing, while Colton’s contract provided the same one-year protection, worth $275,000 at his initial salary. The extra contract year provides Colton with more long-term stability on paper without requiring UNH to guarantee the remaining value of a five-year deal (A bit of a Red Herring Clause). In other words, the commitment got longer, but the university’s financial risk if it decides to make another change barely moved. The easiest interpretation isn’t that UNH dramatically changed what an athletic director is. Much of the underlying governance remains intact. Colton still reports to the president or designee, receives a $5,000 departmental discretionary account, and can be terminated without cause in exchange for one year of base salary. The larger change is what UNH appears to be asking its AD to focus on and produce. Generate controllable revenue. Raise more money. Stay within budget. Work closely with advancement and finance. Build something over five years. And, if successful, it will be difficult for another school to pull you from Durham. That makes President Chilton’s introductory comments about finding someone with the “vision, experience, and judgment” to navigate a changing Division I landscape feel more telling. title: UNH Patients Win 90% of AI Denial Appeals; Derivative Suit Says Executives Knew - Tech Times
content:
On August 14, Luigi Mangione walked into a Manhattan federal courtroom and told a judge exactly what he had done. With that allocution — "On the morning of Dec. 4, 2024, I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan, and he died" — Mangione entered an open plea to two federal stalking counts resulting in death, the strongest formal legal resolution UnitedHealth Group (NYSE: UNH) has received since the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson 20 months ago. By the day's close, UNH shares ticked up 0.67% to $401.73, a market verdict that one headline risk had narrowed. That same week, separately, an amended shareholder derivative complaint filed August 7 in Minnesota federal court widened UNH's legal exposure on an entirely different axis. The complaint alleges governance failures stretching from September 2021 through July 2025 — centered on claims that UNH executives fraudulently inflated Medicare Advantage revenue by making members appear sicker than they were, that an AI algorithm allegedly denied post-acute care to elderly patients in ways that were reversed on appeal at an extraordinary rate, and that inadequate cybersecurity practices contributed to the healthcare data breach that exposed information on approximately 190 million Americans. Plaintiffs allege the resulting misconduct destroyed $277 billion in shareholder value between December 2024 and August 2025. A Bloomberg and Claims Journal report confirmed the filing. Within hours, Mangione's lawyers filed a separate motion to dismiss his New York state murder charges, arguing his federal plea triggers double jeopardy protections under New York law — opening a new legal front just as the old one seemed to be closing. The complaint's specific figures and the legal mechanisms behind them explain why the stock — despite a powerful Q2 earnings recovery — remains roughly $60 below its 52-week high. Mangione, 28, entered an open plea — meaning no plea agreement, no concessions from prosecutors. He faces a maximum penalty of life in prison. U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett advised Mangione that federal sentencing guidelines suggest a range of approximately 24 to 30 years, but noted she is not bound by those guidelines and may consider the full scope of his conduct at sentencing. Sentencing is scheduled for December 18. In his allocution, Mangione revealed for the first time that he had posed as an investor managing more than $50 billion in assets, emailing UnitedHealthcare leadership to confirm the location of the annual investor conference. "Unlike my previous interactions with insurers, I received an immediate response within an hour," Mangione told the court, a line that drew commentary across the healthcare industry. Thompson's family was in the courtroom. "While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable," the Thompson family said in a statement. Mangione voiced no remorse and repeatedly referenced his concerns about the US healthcare system. New York Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch addressed that posture directly: "To those who idolize Luigi Mangione, I say this: violence is not a cause, murder is not a message, and a killer is certainly not a hero." Within hours of the plea, defense attorney Karen Friedman Agnifilo told reporters her team had moved to dismiss the second-degree murder and weapons charges pending in New York state court. The argument: Mangione has already been prosecuted and convicted of conduct arising from the same event, and New York's criminal procedure law — specifically CPL §40.20 — bars successive prosecutions based on the same underlying conduct. New York's double jeopardy statute is broader than the federal constitutional protection, which under Blockburger v. United States (1932) ordinarily permits separate state and federal prosecutions for the same act. The state case is in the hands of New York Supreme Court Justice Gregory Carro, who previously dismissed terrorism charges against Mangione in September 2025 but kept the second-degree murder count alive. His ruling on the double jeopardy motion will determine whether the state murder trial scheduled to begin September 8 proceeds or is delayed indefinitely. Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg's office has signaled it intends to contest the motion and press forward with the prosecution. Former federal prosecutor Berit Berger, speaking on CNN, assessed the federal sentencing outcome: even with a guilty plea and no mandatory minimum, the federal judge will likely sentence Mangione to life in prison or something close to it. Read more:
UnitedHealth Shatters Estimates as AI Trims Medical Costs by 270 Basis Points The shareholder derivative complaint's most significant allegations are not about the Thompson killing. They are about what plaintiffs claim was a systematic practice of denying post-acute rehabilitation care to elderly Medicare Advantage members using an AI tool called nH Predict, developed by naviHealth, a care management company that Optum — UNH's health services subsidiary — acquired in 2020. According to the complaint and independent legal filings in the Lokken v. UnitedHealth Group class action currently pending in U.S. District Court in Minnesota, the nH Predict system was trained on historical patient data to predict the number of days of post-acute care a Medicare Advantage member would require. UNH employees were instructed to keep actual patient stays within 1% of the algorithm's prediction. When patients needed more care than the model anticipated — as determined by their treating physicians — authorization was denied. The algorithm allegedly carried a 90% error rate in the sense that matters most: roughly 90% of denied claims were reversed when patients — or their families — appealed to federal administrative law judges. According to multiple independent analyses and peer-reviewed research, nH Predict generated denials at a rate that independent human review consistently overturned. The reason the math worked anyway is the mechanism the derivative complaint describes explicitly: management calculated that only approximately 0.2% of policyholders appeal denied claims. For elderly patients discharged prematurely from skilled nursing facilities, appealing requires navigating a multi-step administrative process — often while managing the health crisis that prompted the skilled nursing facility stay in the first place. An algorithm that is medically wrong 90% of the time is still financially optimal if almost no one challenges its output. The amended complaint alleges that UNH executives understood this asymmetry and continued using the system because of it. In March 2026, a federal judge ordered UNH to disclose the nH Predict algorithm's specifications, a significant procedural development in the Lokken litigation. Judge John Tunheim had previously dismissed five of seven counts on Medicare preemption grounds in February 2025 but allowed breach of contract and breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing claims to proceed — and ruled UNH's appeal process was effectively "futile" for plaintiffs, waiving the exhaustion requirement. The Office of Inspector General issued its first major Medicare Advantage compliance program guidance update since 1999 in February 2026, specifically directing insurers to audit denial and reversal rates against physician-only benchmarks. The guidance is voluntary — but its existence signals the regulatory direction of travel. naviHealth was rebranded as Home & Community Care in 2024. The current-generation platforms — OptumReal and PreCheck Prior Authorization — are presented by UNH as a different architecture. The company maintains that AI systems serve as guides, not decision-makers, and that licensed medical directors make final adverse determinations. That distinction is the central contested question in the Lokken case. The derivative complaint is a governance case, distinct from the CalPERS-led securities class action (which alleges securities fraud and is still awaiting a dismissal ruling in Minnesota federal court). A derivative suit is brought on behalf of the corporation itself, against its own directors and officers, for alleged breaches of fiduciary duty. If successful, the remedy is corporate governance reform and executive accountability — not direct payments to shareholders. The complaint identifies three principal allegations. First: Medicare Advantage revenue inflation through diagnostic upcoding. The Medicare Advantage payment system — structured around Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) codes — pays insurers higher monthly rates for members with more complex diagnoses. The complaint alleges UNH made members appear sicker through diagnoses plaintiffs characterize as unnecessary, capturing $8.7 billion in federal funds in 2021 alone. Analysts cited in the complaint estimate that Medicare Advantage audits could result in as much as $20 billion in potential clawbacks if the practice is substantiated. This allegation echoes a separate state-level action filed in May 2026: Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell sued UnitedHealthcare in Suffolk Superior Court, alleging the company defrauded MassHealth — the state's Medicaid program — of at least $100 million by making elderly Senior Care Options enrollees appear more seriously impaired than their actual conditions warranted, in order to secure higher capitation payments. The Massachusetts AG lawsuit alleges this scheme was systematic. Under the Massachusetts False Claims Act, treble damages could raise the state's demand to $300 million. UnitedHealthcare called the complaint "meritless." Second: the derivative complaint alleges UNH misled a federal court regarding data firewalls when it acquired Change Healthcare for $13 billion, and that inadequate cybersecurity practices at Change Healthcare contributed to the February 2024 ransomware attack by the BlackCat group. The breach exposed health and personal data belonging to approximately 190 million Americans — the largest healthcare data breach on record. UNH paid a $22 million ransom to the attackers. Third: the complaint cites an independent audit of the company's HouseCalls program that plaintiffs allege conflicted with public statements about the accuracy of its Medicare Advantage risk-coding practices. UNH has not filed a detailed public response to the August 7 amended complaint. Read more:
UnitedHealth Confirms Recent Cyber Breach Resulted in "Substantial" Amount of Stolen Health Data The fundamental picture at UNH improved dramatically in the second quarter of 2026. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $6.38 — approximately 31% above the analyst consensus estimate of $4.91 — and the medical care ratio fell to 86.7%, down from 89.4% in Q2 2025, the single largest operational signal of the quarter. These results are confirmed in the UNH Q2 2026 SEC filing. Operating earnings climbed 55% year-over-year to $8.0 billion. Management raised its full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to a range of $19.50 to $20.00, up from the prior guidance of greater than $18.25, and doubled the share buyback authorization to at least $5.0 billion for the year. Analyst sentiment following the Q2 results was broadly constructive. Bank of America raised its price target to $512 from $475; Truist moved to $500 from $480; RBC Capital raised to $478 from $463; JPMorgan raised its target to $516 from $466; Bernstein reaffirmed a Buy as recently as August 12. The consensus average across analysts tracked by Stockanalysis.com stood at approximately $475, implying roughly 18% upside from the current $401 level. The board authorized a quarterly cash dividend of $2.32 per share on August 12, payable September 22 to shareholders of record as of September 14 — an annualized rate of $9.28 per share. Institutional flows around the stock remained mixed heading into the week. The University of Texas/Texas A&M Investment Management Company disclosed the sale of 11,152 shares in a filing dated August 16 — a modest reduction from a large institutional holder. Midwest Trust Co. disclosed the acquisition of 15,846 additional shares in a Monday filing, according to regulatory filings. Institutional investors collectively hold approximately 87.86% of UNH's outstanding shares. Separately, Berkshire Hathaway — which had held a substantial UNH position — fully exited the stock during Q1 2026, according to filings from the period covering Greg Abel's first quarter as CEO. The stock's 52-week range — from a low of $255.96 to a high of $461.62 — captures the full arc of the post-Thompson killing collapse and partial recovery. At $401, UNH sits roughly 60 points below its 52-week high and roughly 145 points above its trough. The operational story — improving MCR, raised guidance, buyback expansion — supports continued recovery. The legal story — derivative complaint, Massachusetts AG suit, Mangione state trial, CalPERS securities class action — provides the ceiling. The derivative complaint and the Lokken litigation combine to put the AI prior authorization question at the center of the UNH story in a way that the earnings recovery alone does not resolve. The question for both investors and the 49 million Americans covered by UnitedHealthcare is whether the current-generation OptumReal and PreCheck platforms represent a genuine architectural departure from nH Predict — or a rebranding of the same underlying logic applied to a broader patient population. UNH's reform commitments include a pledge to reduce prior authorization requirements for 30% of services currently requiring advance approval, a Gold Card program that exempts high-performing providers from routine prior authorization requirements, and a commitment to publicly report prior authorization metrics. Nearly 95% of prior authorization requests are now submitted electronically, and roughly half are processed in real time. The OIG's February 2026 guidance, and the Lokken court's algorithm disclosure order, suggest that regulators and the judiciary are moving toward greater transparency requirements regardless of what UNH voluntarily reports. The derivative complaint is the most legally consequential of the current actions because it goes directly at board-level governance — and because its success would mandate systemic structural change rather than a financial settlement that leaves the business model intact. For patients, the most actionable fact in the research record is this: patients who appeal post-acute care denials win at an extraordinary rate — approximately 90% of the time, according to multiple independent sources including peer-reviewed research. The vast majority do not appeal. The derivative complaint argues that gap is not an accident. Mangione pleaded guilty on August 14, 2026, to two federal stalking counts resulting in death — based on his admitted tracking of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson to a Manhattan investor conference before shooting him on December 4, 2024. He entered an open plea, meaning no deal with prosecutors. He faces a maximum penalty of life in prison. Federal sentencing guidelines suggest approximately 24 to 30 years, but Judge Margaret Garnett is not bound by those guidelines and will consider the full scope of his conduct at sentencing. Sentencing is scheduled for December 18, 2026. Mangione also faces a separate New York state second-degree murder charge; his attorneys have filed a motion to dismiss those charges under New York's double jeopardy statute, arguing the federal plea bars a second prosecution for the same conduct. State prosecutors have said they intend to fight the motion. A decision from New York Supreme Court Justice Gregory Carro will determine whether the state trial scheduled for September 8 proceeds. The amended derivative complaint, filed August 7 in U.S. District Court in Minnesota, is a governance lawsuit brought on behalf of UnitedHealth Group as a corporation against its own current and former directors and officers. Unlike the CalPERS-led securities class action — which alleges that shareholders were directly defrauded through misleading statements — the derivative complaint seeks to hold executives personally liable for governance failures and to force structural reforms. Its core allegations include: fraudulent Medicare Advantage upcoding that plaintiffs allege captured approximately $8.7 billion in federal payments in 2021 alone; the use of an AI algorithm (nH Predict) that plaintiffs say denied post-acute care at a rate reversed on appeal approximately 99.7% of the time, while management calculated that most patients would not appeal; cybersecurity failures at Change Healthcare that led to a breach affecting 190 million Americans; and alleged misrepresentations to a federal court during the Change Healthcare acquisition. Plaintiffs allege this cascade of misconduct wiped out more than $277 billion in shareholder value between December 2024 and August 2025. The gap between UNH's fundamental recovery and its stock price reflects the legal discount the market is applying. The Q2 earnings beat — adjusted EPS of $6.38 vs. the $4.91 consensus, MCR at 86.7% down from 89.4% — confirms the operational improvement is real. But the stock faces simultaneous legal overhangs: the derivative complaint (governance liability), the CalPERS securities class action (securities fraud), the Massachusetts AG Medicaid fraud lawsuit (potential $300 million with treble damages), the Lokken AI denial class action (ongoing), multiple DOJ investigations into Medicare Advantage practices, and the unresolved question of the Mangione state trial. Analyst price targets cluster around $475 to $516, implying the market sees meaningful upside if the legal picture stabilizes — but at $401, it is pricing in continued legal uncertainty as the primary constraint on valuation. Any Medicare Advantage member denied a service — including post-acute care such as skilled nursing facility stays — has the right to appeal. title: CNC, UNH, CVS, HUM Stocks Slip After-Hours — Trump Administration Reportedly Seeks To Scrap Subsidies On Certain Medicare Plans - Stocktwits
content: Shares of health insurance companies, including Centene (CNC), slipped after-hours on Tuesday following a report that the Trump administration plans to end a federal subsidy program that has helped suppress Medicare Part D prescription drug plan premiums. The federal program is currently channeling an estimated $3.6 billion to insurers this year to keep Part D premiums in check. Officials told The Wall Street Journal that the support will expire after 2026 and will not be extended into 2027. The Journal states that about 25 million Americans are enrolled in Part D plans, with the average monthly premium this year running near $36. The Wall Street Journal reports the decision could leave many seniors confronting higher premiums for their stand-alone prescription coverage beginning in 2027. Without the federal support, plan sponsors may pass increased costs to enrollees, potentially accelerating shifts toward Medicare Advantage plans that bundle drug benefits. An administration official quoted by the Journal projected that roughly one-quarter of Part D enrollees will see their premiums hold steady or decline in 2027, about 30% will face hikes under $10 a month, and the remaining 45% will largely see increases in the $11–$20 range. The subsidy primarily benefits insurers offering stand-alone Part D plans (PDPs). Companies with substantial PDP enrollment—UnitedHealth Group (UNH), CVS Health (CVS, via Aetna), Humana (HUM), Centene (CNC, via WellCare), and Molina Healthcare (MOH)—stand to lose this revenue stream. Loss of the $3.6-billion in support could pressure margins if insurers absorb costs or reduce competitiveness through higher premiums, risking enrollment declines. However, beneficiaries might also migrate to Medicare Advantage plans and help offset losses. Centene holds the largest share of stand-alone Medicare Part D (PDP) enrollment via Wellcare — more than eight million members as of early 2026, or about one-third of the entire PDP market, exceeding the exposure of its rivals. CNC shares dived 3% after hours on Tuesday, while shares of UNH, CVS, and HUM fell by about or less than 1%. In a major bid to accelerate American dominance in the commercial space sector, the Trump administration announced a proposal allowing the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to bypass lengthy environmental reviews for rocket launches, spacecraft reentries, and commercial launch site approvals. The initiative, announced on Tuesday by Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy, aims to eliminate red tape for commercial operators as the U.S. prepares for an unprecedented surge in orbital launches and space infrastructure development. Commercial space stocks, including Rocket Lab (RKLB), AST SpaceMobile (ASTS), Intuitive Machines (LUNR), and Planet Labs (PL) dropped between 3% and 7% on Tuesday, while SpaceX (SPCX) added 3%. Under the proposed framework, the FAA would gain the authority to waive requirements established across 13 major federal environmental statutes. These include the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Clean Air Act. Federal officials emphasized that exemptions would only apply where environmental rules delay innovation, maintaining that core public health, national security, and safety safeguards will remain intact. "America won the first Space Race, and we can do it again -- but only if we get government red tape out of the way," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated, noting that the goal is to lower costs and strengthen U.S. competitiveness. Environmental assessments—which currently can take over a year to complete—have long been a target of frustration for commercial launch providers. While conservation groups view these evaluations as crucial for protecting coastal wildlife habitats, launch companies have repeatedly slammed the reviews as duplicative administrative bottlenecks. The FAA's proposal opens a 30-day public comment window before final rules are enacted. The drive to deregulate comes as the commercial space industry experiences exponential growth. The FAA reported authorizing a record 204 commercial space operations in FY2025. Over the next decade, federal forecasts project total operations could reach over 4,200, climbing from 214 this year to more than 500 annual operations by 2036. Much of this growth is being driven by heavyweights like Elon Musk’s SpaceX, Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, and rising startups like Stoke Space. These firms are aggressively deploying satellite constellations for broadband connectivity, defense applications, and orbital data centers. Rocket Lab (RKLB) made massive waves in the market after announcing an $8-billion acquisition of Iridium Communications. The deal hands Rocket Lab an operational 66-satellite network, global L-band spectrum, and 2.55 million active subscribers, firmly establishing it as the primary commercial competitor to SpaceX. AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) confirmed its next-generation BlueBird 8, 9, and 10 satellites are fully operational in orbit, while SpaceX recently cleared its FAA mishap investigation for Starship Flight 12, paving the way for Flight 13 as it prepares for up to 44 orbital launches annually from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Lucid, based in California, already maintains close links to Saudi Arabia through its majority shareholder, the Public Investment Fund. PIF holds a majority stake of around 57% in Lucid Group, according to a company filing from late April. The stake is held primarily through Ayar Third Investment Company, a wholly owned PIF subsidiary. Earlier this month, Lucid rejected reports that it was considering bankruptcy or a take-private transaction, noting that it has sufficient liquidity to carry its operations well into next year. The company also delivered a cease and desist letter to the publication that carried the bankruptcy rumors, stating that the company “unequivocally denies the central factual assertions” in the article. Lucid is now slated to provide a further update on its financials in its second-quarter earnings call scheduled for August 4. The company, however, has faced significant headwinds. Earlier this month, the company reported second-quarter production of 4,774 vehicles and deliveries of 3,953 units— marking a modest year-over-year increase but short of analyst expectations amid slower-than-hoped demand for the new Gravity SUV. Financially, Lucid continues to face steep losses and negative gross margins despite revenue growth. The company is currently attempting to ramp up growth under the leadership of CEO Silvio Napoli, who assumed the role in June. Napoli undertook a leadership overhaul recently and replaced CFO Taoufiq Boussaid with automotive finance veteran Alexander De Bock. He also appointed new executives for technology, customer, digital, and transformation roles, flattened the reporting structure by halving direct reports to the CEO, and eliminated the COO position. These moves followed June layoffs of roughly 1,500 employees, about 18% of the workforce, and the removal of a second production shift at the Arizona plant, aimed at delivering roughly $158 million in annual savings. The company has relied heavily on its PIF for support through it all. In late April 2026, Ayar purchased $550 million of Lucid’s Series C convertible preferred stock and expanded Lucid’s delayed-draw term loan facility by $500 million. Most recently, on July 6, Lucid drew $800 million under those existing facilities, converting committed credit into immediate cash.
